explanations.explanation: That's the whole request. The Greeks tell Philip, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” (John 12:21) No speech, no warm-up, just the ask. I wish every order at my bakery came in that clear.
Nobody mentions the high priest here. What they say to Philip is, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” (John 12:21) Nobody asks for a meeting with anyone else. They walk up with one name, and it's His.

explanations.answer: To find a place to stay
explanations.explanation: They did go up to worship at the feast (John 12:20), so lodging might cross your mind. But what they ask Philip is, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” (John 12:21) Rooms and beds never come up. I once lived in the back of a junk drawer, so I know a good place to sleep matters, but it isn't their request.

That's right. Philip relayed the appeal to Andrew, and “both of them went and told Jesus.” (John 12:22) So the request didn't stop with Andrew. Two disciples walk it over together, and nobody carries it alone.

This one is true. Philip relayed the appeal to Andrew, and “both of them went and told Jesus.” (John 12:22) The text says nothing about the request getting stuck or put on hold. The two of them take it to Jesus together.

Jesus says, “unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) It sounds backwards, a seed having to die before the good part shows up. But that's exactly how He puts it. The dying is the part He points to.

That's close to the farm, but it's not what Jesus says. He says the kernel “falls to the ground and dies,” and then “it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Harvest never shows up in His picture. The dying is what He names.

Tucking a kernel away sounds careful, but Jesus says unless it dies, “it remains only a seed.” (John 12:24) The kernel has to fall to the ground and die, and then it bears much fruit. A kernel kept safe on a shelf, friend, is just a very well-protected kernel.

Jesus says the opposite of that sentence. “Whoever loves his life will lose it, but whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.” (John 12:25) Those are strong words, and I won't pretend they aren't. But the order is right there in the text: loving his life is the one that loses it.

Right, it gets flipped. “Whoever loves his life will lose it, but whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.” (John 12:25) It's a strong way to say it, and it sounds backwards the first time through. Backwards happens a lot in this passage, friend.

“If anyone serves Me, he must follow Me; and where I am, My servant will be as well.” (John 12:26) In Jesus' words, serving and following go together. And the promise that comes with it is about being right where He is. That's a warm promise to hear.

Saying thanks is a good thing, but it isn't the word here. Jesus says, “If anyone serves Me, he must follow Me.” (John 12:26) Then He adds, “where I am, My servant will be as well.” The word He picks is follow.

Fear isn't in this sentence. Jesus says, “If anyone serves Me, he must follow Me; and where I am, My servant will be as well.” (John 12:26) The word is follow, and the promise after it is about being where He is. I think that sounds more like an invitation than a scare.

Jesus says, “If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor him.” (John 12:26) The honor comes from the Father. That's good news for anyone serving when nobody is clapping. I've stamped plenty of cookies with an empty kitchen watching, so I like that one.

The crowd is standing around in this passage, but Jesus doesn't name them here. He says, “If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor him.” (John 12:26) Applause is nice, but the one He names is the Father. That's where the honor comes from.

Angels do come up a little later, when some in the crowd say an angel spoke (John 12:29). But they aren't who Jesus names here. He says, “If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor him.” (John 12:26) The honor comes from the Father, and I'd take that over any trophy on my shelf.
Jesus says, “Now My soul is troubled.” (John 12:27) He says it out loud, honestly, with no act. I think this part is heavy, and I'm not going to joke on it. We can just let it be what it is.

Jesus says the opposite. His words are, “Now My soul is troubled.” (John 12:27) He doesn't put on a calm face for the people around Him. I think this is a heavy moment, so I'd rather sit with it than hurry past it.
That isn't what He says. His words are, “Now My soul is troubled, and what shall I say?” (John 12:27) He says it plainly. I think this is a heavy moment, so I'll go gently.

Not quite, friend. Jesus wonders out loud whether to ask the Father to save Him from this hour, and then He answers it Himself: “No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour.” (John 12:27) So He doesn't ask for that. What He asks is, “Father, glorify Your name!” (John 12:28)

That's right. Jesus wonders about asking the Father to save Him from this hour, then says, “No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour.” (John 12:27) His actual request goes another direction: “Father, glorify Your name!” (John 12:28) Wondering out loud and asking are two different things.
Right after Jesus asks, “a voice came from heaven.” (John 12:28) The voice says, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” That's what follows His request, in the text's own order.

The text doesn't mention any shaking ground. Right after Jesus asks the Father to glorify His name, “a voice came from heaven.” (John 12:28) The voice says, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” What the passage gives us is a voice.

Fire is a real thing in the Bible, like when the fire of the LORD fell for Elijah (1 Kings 18:38). It's not what shows up here, though. After Jesus asks, “a voice came from heaven,” and it says, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” (John 12:28)

Some in the crowd said it had thundered, and others said that “an angel had spoken to Him.” (John 12:29) Same sound, two guesses. Crowds do that. I do it myself when the oven timer goes off in the other room.

A prophet isn't one of the guesses. The text gives two, thunder, and that “an angel had spoken to Him.” (John 12:29) Nobody in that crowd says prophet. Two guesses are on the table, and that's all of them.
Elder isn't one of the guesses. The text reports two: that it had thundered, and that “an angel had spoken to Him.” (John 12:29) It's a fine word, friend. It's just not the one this crowd uses.
Jesus says it the other way around. “This voice was not for My benefit, but yours.” (John 12:30) The crowd is standing right there, so He's pointing it straight at them. The voice was for them.

That's right. “This voice was not for My benefit, but yours.” (John 12:30) Jesus says it to the same crowd that had been guessing thunder and angels. The voice was for them, and I like that He tells them so plainly.
“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.” (John 12:32) Everyone, friend. Not a few, not one group. The word is everyone, and that's a wide-open door.

Jesus doesn't say He'll leave the world behind. He says, “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.” (John 12:32) The action is drawing. And the word that stands out is everyone.
The twelve tribes aren't mentioned here. Jesus says, “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.” (John 12:32) The word is everyone. That's wider than any one group.

The writer tells us, “He said this to indicate the kind of death He was going to die.” (John 12:33) So when Jesus talks about being lifted up, He's pointing to how He will die. I think this is a heavy part. I'll let the text say it and leave it there.

This one is true. The writer says, “He said this to indicate the kind of death He was going to die.” (John 12:33) Jesus' words about being lifted up point to how He will die. I think it's a heavy line, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: Who this Son of Man is
explanations.explanation: They ask, “Who is this Son of Man?” (John 12:34) It comes right after they wonder how the Son of Man can be lifted up when they've heard from the Law that “the Christ will remain forever.” Honestly, fair question. I'd ask it too.

They do talk about the Christ, but they don't ask when He's coming. They say that from the Law they've heard “the Christ will remain forever,” and then they ask, “Who is this Son of Man?” (John 12:34) That's a who question. Timing never comes up.

explanations.answer: Where He plans to go next
explanations.explanation: They don't ask about travel plans. After wondering how the Son of Man can be lifted up, they ask, “Who is this Son of Man?” (John 12:34) That's a who question, not a where. I think they're more stuck on the name than on the road map.

Jesus says, “Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you.” (John 12:35) Then He adds, “The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going.” Light and dark are the two pictures He uses. I'd rather walk with the lights on.

Sorrow is a real word, but it's not in this verse. Jesus says, “Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you.” (John 12:35) The thing that could overtake them is darkness. Light and dark are the two pictures He uses.

Fear isn't the word in this verse. Jesus says, “Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you.” (John 12:35) What could overtake them is darkness. He keeps the picture simple: the Light, or the dark.

Jesus says the opposite of waiting. He tells them, “Walk while you have the Light,” (John 12:35) and then, “While you have the Light, believe in the Light.” (John 12:36) The time He points to is now, while they still have the Light. He doesn't tell them to hold off.

That's right. Jesus tells them, “While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light.” (John 12:36) He says to do it while they have the Light, not to put it off until later. The word that matters is while.

“While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light.” (John 12:36) Believing in the Light is the step, and becoming sons of light is where it leads. It's a lovely line, and I'll admit I like anything with light in it. My ovens do glow.

That isn't what Jesus says. The crowd had just talked about the Law (John 12:34), but His answer here is about light. He says, “While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light.” (John 12:36)

That phrase isn't in this passage. Jesus says, “While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light.” (John 12:36) The picture He uses is light. It's good to stick with the words He actually picks.

explanations.answer: He goes away and is hidden from them
explanations.explanation: After Jesus had spoken these things, “He went away and was hidden from them.” (John 12:36) It's a quiet exit. No big announcement, just a Jesus who spoke and then stepped away from the crowd.

explanations.answer: He stays and heals the sick among them
explanations.explanation: Healing isn't mentioned in this stretch of the passage. After Jesus had spoken, “He went away and was hidden from them.” (John 12:36) That's what the text says He does next. He doesn't stay.

explanations.answer: He goes up to teach in the temple
explanations.explanation: Teaching in the temple isn't what happens right after. Once Jesus had spoken these things, “He went away and was hidden from them.” (John 12:36) That's the next thing the text says. He leaves instead of staying to teach.
